background.definition: A congenital umbilical hernia is a fascial defect at the umbilicus, presenting before 6 months of age.

list.listitem: The reported incidence of umbilical hernia for all children varies widely, but overall ranges from 10% to 15%.
The incidence is 25% to 50% in African-American children and 4% to 9% in Caucasian children.
The incidence is higher in premature infants than in term infants, and slightly more common in males.
An umbilical hernia develops when the umbilical ring fails to close after cord separation.
Genetic component. Family history of surgically treated umbilical hernia in a sibling is a risk factor (familial concordant standardized incidence ratio 3.61 [95% CI, 3.33-3.91]).

Authors of a genome-wide association study including 62,637 UK Biobank participants with either single or multiple hernia phenotypes (inguinal, femoral, umbilical and hiatal) identified strong evidence for 5 shared susceptibility loci and 28 independent (seven previously unreported) shared susceptibility loci which clustered in functional categories related to connective tissue and elastic fiber homeostasis.
In most children, the umbilical ring will diminish in size and close by age 4 years.
The hernia sac contains omentum and/or portions of small intestine.
Once closed, recurrence is uncommon.
Diagnosis is clinical. Children present with a soft, umbilical protuberance covered by skin, usually easily reducible. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Hernia sac covered by peritoneum, rather than overlying skin
Inflammation/erythema and edema of the umbilical skin
Beefy red tissue in the umbilicus
Beefy red tissue in the umbilicus, also called an umbilical polyp

list.listitem: Soft umbilical protuberance, covered by skin, and easily reducible through the fibrous ring at the umbilicus. The borders of the fascial defect can be easily palpated through the skin.
Hernia protuberance is less noticeable at rest, in supine position; the protuberance is more noticeable when the child is crying, coughing, or straining during a bowel movement.
The hernia usually causes no apparent symptoms for the child.
Estimates of hernia size, including clinical and intraoperative assessments, appear to be only weakly to moderately correlated.
The diagnosis of an uncomplicated umbilical hernia is clinical, based on physical examination and history.
Similarly, the diagnosis of a complicated umbilical hernia is clinical, with an irreducible and painful umbilical mass.
The European Hernia Society and Americas Hernia Society (EHS/AHS) guideline (2020) suggests imaging by ultrasound or computed tomography if the diagnosis is in doubt, based on weak evidence.
See algorithm in .
Immediate surgery is indicated for a preceding history of an irreducible umbilical hernia and localized umbilical tenderness. A
Asymptomatic, persistent umbilical hernias with 2.0 cm or greater fascial defects should be repaired between the ages of 4 and 5 years. B
Reducing the hernia by strapping the skin does not accelerate healing or prevent incarcerations. C
Elective operative repair is generally done when the child is 4 to 5 years old, when fascial defects are the smallest.
In the child, infraumbilical incision with removal of the hernia sac and simple transverse repair of the fascial defect is recommended. Repair can be open or laparoscopic.
A single perioperative dose of antibiotics is suggested when mesh is used for umbilical hernia repair by the EHS/AHS guideline.
Postoperative complications of umbilical hernia repair are uncommon, but include wound infection, seroma and/or hematoma formation, bowel injury, and recurrence.

In a case series of 186 patients undergoing open laparoscopic hernia repair with fascial defect closure and intraperitoneal onlay mesh fixation at a single institution, there were no recurrences at average follow-up of 16.5 ± 17.7 months. Postoperative complications included wound erythema (2.7%), hematomas (1.1%), and seromas (2.7%).

Authors of a systematic review of 9 papers found local anesthesia for umbilical hernia to be feasible with no conversions to general anesthesia described and 90% of patients were discharged home within 24 hours compared to 47% following general anesthesia. Patient satisfaction rates was high (89% to 97%) and complications were uncommon and included site infection (3.4%) and recurrence (2% to 7.4%).

Use of a transversus abdominis plane block performed better than wound infiltration with local anesthetic for 2-hour post-operative rest-pain score among patients undergoing inguinal or infra-umbilical hernia repair, based on a meta-analysis of 7 trials including 420 patients. No complications were reported.

Similar results were demonstrated in an RCT including 72 patients undergoing open umbilical hernia repair for patients with cirrhotic ascites. In this study, rectus sheath block outperformed local infiltration for intraoperative remedial analgesia, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and pain scores during post-operative activity

For pediatric umbilical hernia repair, rectus sheath block was comparable to local anesthetic for immediate and 1-hour post-operative analgesia with no differences in post-operative nausea based on a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs.

listitem.strong: Laparoscopic vs. open repair and fascial defect closure or not

list.listitem: In a retrospective cohort study of 14,652 patients undergoing umbilical hernia repair, laparoscopic repair was performed in 10.5% and was associated with fewer wound complications (Odds ratio [OR] 0.41; 95% CI, 0.20-0.78) but longer operative time (57.7 min vs. 38.3 min), longer length of stay (0.29 days vs. 0.17 days), and an increased rate of respiratory (0.52% vs. 0.10%) and cardiac (0.26% vs. 0.05%) complications.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 3 RCTs and 7 retrospective cohort studies concluded that open repair of umbilical hernias may result in higher risk of wound infection (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.23-4.48), wound dehiscence (OR 4.99, 95% CI 1.12-22.28) and recurrence (OR 4.06, 95% CI 1.54-10.71) compared to laparoscopic repair. However, higher-quality RCTs are needed.

In two RCTs of 100 patients and 80 patients, respectively, who were undergoing laparoscopic umbilical hernia repair with intraperitoneal onlay mesh, those randomized to closure of the fascial defect vs. no closure had significantly reduced seroma formation at 2 weeks (2% vs. 24%, first cited trial) and, for the second cited trial, at 30 days (35% vs. 58%) and cumulative 2-year recurrence (7% vs. 19%) without inducing more side-effects. The recurrence rate for those in the no-closure group, however, is higher than expected.
Umbilicoplasty can be done for larger defects.

The EHS/AHS guideline (2020) recommends mesh for umbilical hernia repair to prevent recurrence. The quality of evidence on mesh is limited for small (<1 cm) defects. Based on weak evidence, this guideline suggests that a permanent mesh should be placed in the preperitoneal space for open umbilical repair. Consideration of laparoscopic repair is suggested for large umbilical hernias or if the patient has an increased risk of wound infection.

In adults, operative repair with mesh is associated with a lower recurrence rate compared with primary repair and similar complication rates. In an RCT of 300 patients with small umbilical hernias, use of mesh reduced rates of recurrence at 2 years (6 vs. 17 treated with sutures only; number needed to treat 13, 95% CI 7-56) with similar rates of complications—seroma (3% vs. <1%), hematoma (2% vs. 1%), and wound infection (2% vs. 1%) for mesh versus suture repair, respectively.

In a meta-analysis of 9 studies, mesh repair was associated with a small reduction in recurrence rates compared with suture repairs for primary ventral hernias, including umbilical hernias, but an increased risk of seroma and surgical site infection.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs confirmed that mesh repair reduced recurrence risk compared with sutured repair (RR 0.28, 95% confidence interval 0.13-0.58) for umbilical hernias with defects between 1 and 4 cm. Although there appeared to be no difference in complication rates, lack of data precluded meta-analysis for several outcomes including seroma formation and quality of life.

In a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs with 620 patients, open mesh repair significantly reduced the incidence of recurrence (OR 0.22, CI 0.10-0.48) without increasing risk of wound infection, seroma or hematoma formation. Reduced recurrence risk with use of mesh (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.13-0.53) was also found in a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 742 patients undergoing elective umbilical hernia repair also with no increased risk of wound infection, seroma or hematoma formation.

Ventral patch repair - a self-expanding, partially absorbable, flexible laminate mesh device – was compared with flat polypropylene mesh in an RCT of 348 adult Dutch patients with symptomatic, primary umbilical or epigastric hernia. Use of the patch resulted in a 5-minute faster operative time, similar total complication rates (24.9% for PVP and 18.7% for mesh), more early reoperations (2.8% vs. 0%, respectively), and a trend towards higher recurrence rates (7.8% vs. 3.3%, respectively, p=.08). In the US, there have been several recalls of the device due to the device coating delaminating and a recent lawsuit against the company’s surgical mesh implant for pelvic organ prolapse repair.

In an RCT of 348 adults with primary small umbilical or epigastric hernia, those randomized to a flat polypropylene mesh repair compared to patch repair had lower rates of complications within 2 years (22.1% vs. 32.5%, respectively) and reoperation (4% vs. 10.7%) but similar rates of recurrence (4.2% vs. 8.4%).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials at moderate to high-risk of bias were unable to determine if any mesh fixation technique (e.g., absorbable or nonabsorbable tacks or sutures) was superior to any other.

To control post-operative pain, one study of 52 children undergoing elective umbilical hernia repair demonstrated that those randomized to bilateral rectus sheath block had lower median FACES Pain Rating Scale scores and decreased use of opioid and non-opioid medications compared with children randomized to local anesthetic infiltration.
Postoperative pressure dressing is not needed to prevent hematoma formation.
Despite no available comparative data, watchful waiting can be considered for patients with asymptomatic umbilical or epigastric hernias.

Adhesive strapping of infant umbilical hernias, changed weekly, may be an alternative to observation. Authors of a case series of 89 Japanese infants reported complete closure after 2 to 13 weeks of strapping in 81 infants (91%); strapping was discontinued in 5 infants (5.6%) due to severe skin complications.
Irreducible hernia is the main complication of umbilical hernia and requires urgent evaluation and surgical treatment.
Children with persistent, asymptomatic, reducible umbilical hernias with defects more than 2.0 cm at age 5 years should be referred for surgical repair.

Proboscoid umbilical hernias are an important subset. The fascial defects are similar to other umbilical hernias; however, these umbilical hernias have an excessive amount of overlying skin that can create social or cosmetic concerns for the parents. Early repair can be considered in this group.

Complications of umbilical hernias include irreducibility, bowel obstruction, or strangulation. Patients usually present with umbilical pain with a tender irreducible mass palpated by the umbilicus. Complications require urgent surgery.
Umbilical hernia size is not related to incidence of complications.
One prospective series reported a 7% incidence of complications requiring surgical repair.
Strangulation is rare at 0.07% (7 per 10,000). With strangulation, the bowel can become necrosed and perforate, requiring resection.
By age 5 years, 95% of umbilical hernias with fascial defects of less than 1 cm in size will diminish in size and close with no treatment. B
The most common complication of umbilical hernia is irreducibility associated with pain, and this has an incidence as high as 7%. C

In a large national surgical database of umbilical hernia repair in adults without ascites and/or esophageal varices, postoperative mortality was 0.1% and morbidity was 3.9%. Types of morbidity primarily included wound infection, pneumonia, and sepsis. Among the 390 patients with ascites/esophageal varices, mortality was 5.1% and morbidity 13.1%. There were significantly higher rates of postoperative sepsis (10.7% vs. 2.9% among other adults), failure to wean, and return to the operating room among patients with ascites/varices.

Predictors of 30-day mortality in a study of 688 patients with ascites undergoing umbilical hernia repair were preoperative Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score, albumin, white blood cell count, and platelet count.
Recurrence rates for umbilical hernia range from about 3% to 10% depending on clinical risk factors and type of repair as noted above.

In a retrospective VA study, hernia recurrence following repair did not appear to be related to weight (3.7% among obese patients vs. 4.6% among non-obese patients); however, in another retrospective VA study, obesity and ascites were both risk factors for recurrence.

In a Danish population study of 244 women who underwent umbilical or epigastric hernia repair and subsequently became pregnant, cumulative recurrence rate was 16.3% after mesh repair and 10.9% after suture repair.

In a retrospective cohort of 126 pregnant women with umbilical hernias requiring repair over 10 years, most (95%) underwent open repair, 58% had an incarcerated or strangulated hernia at surgery, and the most common morbidity was superficial surgical site infection.
